subtopic_detail: Radiographic hip surveillance interval in a non ambulant child with spastic cerebral palsy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a complex care clinic reviewing a 5 year old girl with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy. She has never taken independent steps, is transported in a moulded seating system and needs support to sit.

Her parents say she seems comfortable, sits happily in her chair through a school day and does not cry with nappy changes or dressing. Passive hip abduction is 45 degrees on each side with no fixed deformity and her legs are the same length. Her last pelvic radiograph was at eighteen months of age and reported no abnormality. She has had no hip imaging since, because she has never complained of pain.

data_table.Examination: Passive hip abduction 45 degrees bilaterally, no leg length discrepancy, no pain on hip range of movement, unable to sit unsupported
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic radiograph at eighteen months of age reported as normal, no imaging since

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management of her hips?

options.text: Pelvic radiograph now and every six months with migration percentage measured
options.rationale: A child who cannot walk sits in the highest risk group for progressive hip displacement, and Australian surveillance schedules call for six monthly radiographs with measured migration percentage from two years of age through the years of fastest displacement (Source: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy).
source_refs: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy

options.text: Pelvic radiograph only when hip pain or loss of abduction is noticed
options.rationale: Displacement is silent until it is advanced, and waiting for pain or restricted abduction means most hips are already beyond the range in which preventive surgery works (Source: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy).
source_refs: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips now and again at skeletal maturity
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging characterises cartilage and soft tissue but is not the surveillance instrument, since the decision rule is built on a measurement taken from a standardised plain radiograph (Source: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy).
source_refs: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips every six months to avoid repeated radiation
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the tool for the infant hip before the femoral head ossifies, and by five years the ossified head makes it unreliable for measuring displacement (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Refer for botulinum toxin to the hip adductors and review clinically in a year
options.rationale: Adductor injection can help spasticity and positioning but does not prevent displacement, and using it in place of imaging removes the measurement that triggers timely surgery (Source: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy).
source_refs: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy

explanation.summary: Hip displacement occurs in about a third of children with cerebral palsy overall and in the large majority of those who never walk, and it is a mechanical consequence of muscle imbalance rather than a congenital abnormality. The risk is stratified by gross motor function, so surveillance frequency is set by motor level rather than by symptoms: children who walk independently need little or no radiographic follow up, while non ambulant children are imaged six monthly through early childhood. Migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying outside the bony acetabulum, is the measured variable, and a value above 30 per cent or an increase of more than 10 per cent a year triggers orthopaedic referral. Detected early, displacement is managed with soft tissue surgery, while a dislocated painful hip in adolescence requires major reconstructive or salvage surgery and causes lasting pain and difficulty with seating and hygiene. Pain is a late and unreliable signal, and many children with communication difficulty cannot report it at all.
key_points: Surveillance frequency is set by gross motor function, not by symptoms.
Non ambulant children need six monthly pelvic radiographs through early childhood.
Migration percentage above 30 per cent or a rise above 10 per cent a year triggers orthopaedic referral.
Hip displacement is silent until advanced, so waiting for pain forfeits preventive surgery.
Ultrasound is the infant tool and is unreliable once the femoral head has ossified.
explanation.pearls: Migration percentage rising more than 10 percentage points in a year predicts progression to dislocation more reliably than any single absolute value, so serial measurements on comparable radiographs matter more than the number on any one film.

sources.label: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy
RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

subtopic_detail: Interpreting raised transaminases of muscle origin in a boy with motor delay
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver blood tests found while investigating tiredness. He walked at 19 months and his mother says he still cannot keep up in the playground and asks to be carried home from kindergarten.

To stand from sitting on the floor he rolls onto his front, pushes up onto his hands and feet and then walks his hands up his thighs. His calves feel firm and look larger than expected for his build. He speaks in short sentences and his kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about his language. Abdominal examination finds no hepatomegaly, an abdominal ultrasound is normal and his gamma glutamyl transferase is within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Rises from the floor by climbing up his own legs, waddling gait, firm enlarged calves, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 310 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 285 U/L (less than 45), gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits, creatine kinase 14200 U/L (less than 200), abdominal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with electromyography of the proximal muscles
options.rationale: Electrodiagnostic testing separates neuropathic from myopathic weakness, a question already answered by a creatine kinase in the tens of thousands, and it is uncomfortable for a preschool child (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunohistochemistry and western blot
options.rationale: Biopsy is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is negative or ambiguous, since it requires anaesthesia in a child with a myopathy and adds nothing when the mutation is identifiable on blood (Source: RCH Melbourne: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy to characterise the raised transaminase pattern
options.rationale: Alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are present in skeletal muscle as well as liver, and a normal gamma glutamyl transferase with a normal ultrasound points away from hepatic disease entirely (Source: RCH Melbourne: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain to investigate the language delay
options.rationale: Cognitive and language delay accompanies this condition in about a third of boys because the gene product is expressed in brain, so the delay is explained rather than requiring separate imaging (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene for deletions and duplications
options.rationale: Deletions or duplications of one or more exons account for about three quarters of cases and are identified on a blood sample, so molecular testing confirms the diagnosis, defines the mutation for treatment eligibility and enables carrier testing in the family (Source: RCH Melbourne: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is frequently diagnosed late, and one of the commonest detours is an incidental finding of raised transaminases that leads to a hepatic workup, because clinicians forget that these enzymes are abundant in skeletal muscle. Requesting a creatine kinase alongside any unexplained transaminase elevation in a boy is the step that redirects the investigation. Clinical clues are motor delay, a waddling gait, difficulty with stairs, calf pseudohypertrophy and the characteristic manoeuvre of climbing up the legs to stand from the floor. Cognitive and language delay occur in about a third and are part of the condition. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids prolong ambulation, cardiac and respiratory surveillance begins in childhood, mutation specific therapies depend on knowing the exact variant, and the family needs genetic counselling since about two thirds of mothers are carriers.
key_points: Raised alanine and aspartate aminotransferase with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase can be muscle in origin.
Check creatine kinase in any boy with unexplained transaminase elevation or motor delay.
Genetic testing on blood identifies about three quarters of cases and has displaced biopsy as the first test.
Cognitive and language delay affects about a third and is part of the condition.
Diagnosis unlocks corticosteroid therapy, cardiac surveillance and family genetic counselling.
explanation.pearls: Creatine kinase in this condition runs at ten to a hundred times the upper limit of normal from birth, so a value in the tens of thousands in a boy with motor delay is close to diagnostic before any genetic result returns.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

subtopic_detail: Timing the first retinal examination in an extremely preterm infant
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar on the special care nursery round. A girl born at 24 weeks and 2 days gestation weighing 620 g is now 28 days old and stable on continuous positive airway pressure in 25 per cent oxygen.

Her mother asks when her daughter's eyes will be checked, because a friend's baby had eye examinations in hospital. The infant received supplemental oxygen from birth, has had two courses of antibiotics for suspected sepsis and is tolerating expressed breast milk feeds. Growth is tracking along the third centile for corrected age. No ophthalmology review has been arranged so far.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 52/30 mmHg, respiratory rate 54 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in 25 per cent oxygen, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (140-220 at birth), cranial ultrasound no intraventricular haemorrhage

lead_in: When should her first retinal examination be performed?

options.text: Now, since she has already reached four weeks of postnatal age
options.rationale: Four weeks postnatal age is one half of the rule, but in an extremely preterm infant this arrives at 28 weeks postmenstrual age, before the retinal vasculature has developed enough for the examination to be informative (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: Only if supplemental oxygen is still required beyond 28 days of life
options.rationale: Oxygen exposure modifies risk but screening eligibility is set by gestation and birthweight, and disease occurs in eligible infants who never received prolonged supplemental oxygen (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: At term corrected age, when the retina has completed vascularisation
options.rationale: Treatable disease develops and can progress to retinal detachment well before term, so waiting until 40 weeks misses the window in which laser or intravitreal therapy preserves vision (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: In the week before discharge home, with outpatient follow up afterwards
options.rationale: Screening is timed to the biology of retinal vascularisation rather than to the discharge date, and an infant of this gestation may remain an inpatient for months (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: At 31 weeks postmenstrual age, which for her falls in about three weeks
options.rationale: The first examination occurs at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever comes later, and for an infant born at 24 weeks the postmenstrual criterion is the later of the two (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

explanation.summary: Retinopathy of prematurity results from arrested retinal vascularisation followed by disordered neovascularisation, and it remains a preventable cause of childhood blindness in survivors of extreme prematurity. Australian screening covers infants born before 31 weeks gestation or weighing less than 1250 g at birth, with the first examination at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later. Examinations continue at one to three weekly intervals depending on the zone and stage found, until the retina is fully vascularised or the disease has regressed. Treatment thresholds are defined by zone, stage and the presence of plus disease, and laser photocoagulation or intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor therapy is delivered within days of reaching them. Even treated infants need long term follow up for myopia, strabismus and amblyopia.
key_points: Screen infants born before 31 weeks gestation or weighing under 1250 g.
First examination at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later.
The postmenstrual criterion governs for the most preterm infants, the postnatal one for larger babies.
Repeat examinations continue until full vascularisation or regression.
Treatment thresholds rest on zone, stage and plus disease, and are acted on within days.
explanation.pearls: Plus disease, meaning dilation and tortuosity of the posterior pole vessels, is the feature that converts an observation interval into a treatment decision, and its presence in zone I mandates treatment within about 72 hours.

sources.label: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity
Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity

subtopic_detail: Escalating beyond phototherapy when neurological signs accompany severe hyperbilirubinaemia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department for a 4 day old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and birth. His mother says he has gone a deep yellow colour, has fed poorly since yesterday and has a cry she describes as sharp and different from before.

He was discharged at 36 hours of age when he looked well. Today he is difficult to rouse for a feed, and when you lift him his neck arches backwards and his back stiffens before he settles. Intensive phototherapy was started twenty minutes ago on arrival. His mother is blood group O positive and the baby is A positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 46 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 465 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 12 micromol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (140-220), reticulocytes raised, direct antiglobulin test positive, glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue intensive phototherapy alone and repeat the bilirubin in four hours
options.rationale: Phototherapy lowers bilirubin over hours, and the arched posture with a high pitched cry signals bilirubin already crossing into the brain, so a four hour observation period accepts ongoing neuronal injury (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin and continue intensive phototherapy
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has a role in isoimmune haemolysis where the bilirubin is rising despite phototherapy and approaching the exchange threshold, but it works too slowly to be the answer once encephalopathy is evident (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Stop breastfeeding, give formula feeds and continue intensive phototherapy
options.rationale: Improving enteral intake reduces enterohepatic recirculation and is worth doing, but substituting formula addresses a minor contributor while the acute neurological emergency goes untreated (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Arrange urgent exchange transfusion while intensive phototherapy continues
options.rationale: Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy, here lethargy with retrocollis and a high pitched cry, mandate exchange transfusion irrespective of where the value sits on the treatment chart, and phototherapy runs throughout the preparation (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Commence phenobarbitone to induce hepatic conjugation and observe overnight
options.rationale: Enzyme induction takes days to alter conjugation and has no place in acute severe hyperbilirubinaemia, and sedating an encephalopathic newborn masks the very signs being monitored (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in the first week is managed on a chart that plots the value against postnatal age and risk factors, with separate lines for phototherapy and for exchange transfusion. That chart is overridden by clinical signs: lethargy, hypotonia, a high pitched cry, poor feeding, retrocollis and opisthotonos indicate that unbound bilirubin is already crossing the blood brain barrier, and exchange transfusion becomes immediate regardless of the number. ABO incompatibility with a positive direct antiglobulin test, as here, is a common Australian cause of early haemolytic jaundice in a group O mother, alongside rhesus disease and glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Early discharge before the bilirubin peaks is a recurring contributor, which is why a review within 48 hours of discharge is arranged for babies who go home before 72 hours. Kernicterus, the chronic sequel, produces choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss and upward gaze palsy, and is entirely preventable.
key_points: Neurological signs override the treatment chart and mandate immediate exchange transfusion.
Retrocollis, opisthotonos, a high pitched cry and lethargy are the acute encephalopathy signs.
Continue intensive phototherapy while the exchange is being organised.
Immunoglobulin is for isoimmune haemolysis approaching threshold, not for established encephalopathy.
Discharge before 72 hours requires a review within 48 hours because the bilirubin has not yet peaked.
explanation.pearls: Double volume exchange, about 160 to 180 mL per kilogram, removes roughly 85 per cent of circulating red cells and around half the total body bilirubin in a single procedure, which is why nothing pharmacological substitutes for it once encephalopathy has begun.

subtopic_detail: Managing a self limiting viral skin eruption in a child with coexisting dermatitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 5 year old boy whose mother is upset about spots that keep spreading. They started as three bumps behind his knee eight weeks ago and there are now about thirty across his trunk, arms and both knee creases.

The lesions are 2 to 4 mm, dome shaped, skin coloured and each has a small central dimple. Several sit within patches of dry, scaly, itchy skin that his mother treats intermittently with a moisturiser she buys at the supermarket. He is otherwise well, eats and plays normally, and has not been unwell. His mother has been told by the swimming school that he cannot return until the spots are gone, and she asks you to freeze them off today.

data_table.Examination: Approximately thirty dome shaped umbilicated papules 2 to 4 mm across the trunk, arms and popliteal fossae, surrounding dry scaly erythematous patches, no pustules, no surrounding cellulitis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for ten days to cover secondary bacterial infection
options.rationale: Antibiotics are for secondary infection with pustules, spreading erythema or systemic features, and the surrounding change described here is eczematous rather than infective (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Treat each lesion with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy at today's appointment
options.rationale: Cryotherapy is painful, poorly tolerated in a preschool child and risks hypopigmentation and scarring for a condition that resolves without any treatment (Source: RCH Melbourne: Molluscum contagiosum).

options.text: Prescribe topical imiquimod cream applied three nights a week for sixteen weeks
options.rationale: Randomised evidence shows no benefit over vehicle for this condition in children while producing application site irritation, so it is not recommended despite being widely requested (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Explain the natural course and treat the surrounding dermatitis with topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: The eruption clears spontaneously over months to two years and no exclusion from swimming is required, while treating the surrounding dermatitis reduces scratching, which is what spreads lesions and causes secondary infection (Source: RCH Melbourne: Molluscum contagiosum).

options.text: Refer for curettage of all lesions under general anaesthesia within the month
options.rationale: Anaesthetic risk for a benign self limiting condition is disproportionate, and new lesions typically appear after curettage because the virus is already seeded in adjacent skin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection of the epidermis that spreads by direct contact and by autoinoculation from scratching, and it is one of the commonest reasons a preschool child is brought to a doctor for skin. Lesions are dome shaped, umbilicated papules that appear in crops over months and then resolve completely without scarring, typically within twelve to eighteen months and sometimes up to two years. Children with atopic dermatitis develop more numerous and more widespread lesions because the barrier is impaired and scratching seeds new sites, so treating the dermatitis is the intervention that most reduces spread. An inflammatory reaction with redness and tenderness around lesions commonly heralds resolution and is frequently mistaken for bacterial infection. Australian guidance does not require exclusion from school, childcare or swimming, though covering lesions with clothing or a dressing during swimming is reasonable.
key_points: The eruption is self limiting and resolves without scarring over months to about two years.
Coexisting dermatitis drives spread through scratching, so treating it is the priority.
Exclusion from school, childcare or swimming is not required.
Inflammation around lesions usually signals impending resolution rather than bacterial infection.
Destructive treatments risk scarring and pain for a condition that clears on its own.
explanation.pearls: A crop of lesions turning red, swollen and tender at around the nine to twelve month mark is the beginning of the end rather than a complication, and reassurance at that point prevents an unnecessary course of antibiotics.
